navigation.title: SEF Carbon and Air Quality Explorer

meta.description: Base layer: OpenStreetMap
Base layer: Sentinel-2 cloudless mosaic 2024
Base layer: Terrain Light by EOX

Column-mean CO2 from the CAMS global greenhouse gas forecast, updated three-hourly. This is the layer to open a verification conversation on, because it shows what an operational atmospheric system can say about CO2 today, ahead of the dedicated Copernicus CO2M mission. Data shown: live, the latest step from the rolling CAMS global forecast. Note: the atmospheric CO2 background is around 420 ppm everywhere, so national emissions appear as enhancements of a few ppm on top of a large uniform signal. A total-column map does not attribute emissions to a country or a sector, and it cannot be read as an emissions inventory. Attribution requires inverse modelling that combines these fields with wind and prior emission estimates.

Column-mean methane from the CAMS global greenhouse gas forecast. Methane is the second largest contributor to warming after CO2 and has a short atmospheric lifetime, so cuts show up in the atmosphere within a decade. That is the reasoning behind the Global Methane Pledge target of a 30 per cent cut by 2030 against 2020, and it is why methane is the gas where satellite monitoring is closest to being decision-grade. Data shown: live, the latest step from the rolling CAMS global forecast. Note: this is a model field constrained by satellite observations, not a direct measurement. It resolves regional enhancements over basins and wetlands, not individual facilities.

Column-averaged CO2 retrieved by NASA's OCO-2, shown as the satellite actually sees it. Put this next to the CAMS CO2 field to make the honest point about current capability: OCO-2 has a narrow swath and cannot see through cloud, so a single day over Europe is a few thin ribbons of soundings rather than a map. That gap between what a model can render and what a satellite can measure is the argument for CO2M, which is designed for wide-swath imaging of anthropogenic CO2 plumes. Data shown: fixed at 30 September 2025, the latest date available in GIBS for this product when the config was built. It does not advance on its own. Note: the date is pinned to 30 September 2025. Step it or zoom out to build up coverage. Blank areas mean no retrieval, not zero CO2.

sources.name: Carbon dioxide anomaly against the global mean (OCO-2)

meta.description: The same OCO-2 soundings expressed as a difference from the global mean, which removes the large uniform background and leaves the enhancements and drawdowns. This is the more useful of the two OCO-2 views for a source-and-sink discussion, because positive values sit over emitting regions and negative values over vegetation taking up carbon in the growing season. Data shown: fixed at 30 September 2025, the same single day as the OCO-2 total column layer. It does not advance on its own. Note: same swath and cloud limits as the total column layer. The anomaly is against a global mean, not against a national baseline, so it does not support compliance claims.

Column-averaged dry-air methane from Sentinel-5P TROPOMI, annual mean for 2025 processed by S5P-PAL. Averaging a full year suppresses the retrieval noise that makes single overpasses hard to read, which brings out persistent enhancements over oil and gas basins, coal regions and large wetlands. Data shown: fixed. Annual mean for calendar year 2025, a static file on the SEF bucket that does not update. Note: an annual mean deliberately removes the episodic super-emitter events that dominate short-term methane releases, so this layer answers where methane is persistently elevated, not who vented last week. TROPOMI retrievals are degraded over water, snow and at high latitudes.

attribution.text: Copernicus Sentinel-5P (TROPOMI) / S5P-PAL, processed by S&T, hosted by ESA SEF

meta.description: Tropospheric NO2 column from Sentinel-5P TROPOMI, annual mean for 2025. NO2 is the bridge between the two halves of this explorer. It is a regulated health pollutant in its own right and it is co-emitted with CO2 during high-temperature combustion, so the NO2 pattern traces the fossil fuel activity that the CO2 field cannot resolve. Research on plume-based emission estimation uses exactly this pairing. Data shown: fixed. Annual mean for calendar year 2025, a static file on the SEF bucket that does not update. Note: NO2 has a lifetime of hours, so the map shows where fuel is burned rather than where the resulting CO2 ends up. Column amounts are not surface concentrations and cannot be compared with air quality limit values.

attribution.text: Copernicus Sentinel-5P (TROPOMI) / S5P-PAL, processed by S&T, hosted by ESA SEF

meta.description: Surface PM2.5 from the CAMS European regional ensemble, hourly out to four days ahead. PM2.5 is the pollutant with the clearest link to mortality and it carries the sharpest tightening in the revised Ambient Air Quality Directive (EU) 2024/2881, where the annual limit value falls to 10 µg/m³ from 1 January 2030. The WHO 2021 guideline is 5 µg/m³. Reading the map against those two numbers is the fastest way to see the size of the compliance gap. Data shown: live, the latest hourly step from the CAMS European regional forecast. Note: this is a modelled forecast at roughly 10 km, not a measurement. It cannot resolve a street canyon or a single industrial stack, and formal compliance assessment is done against the reference monitoring network, not against this field.

Surface PM10 from the CAMS European regional ensemble. The annual limit value falls to 20 µg/m³ from 2030 under Directive (EU) 2024/2881. PM10 behaves differently from PM2.5 because a larger share is mechanical in origin, from road and brake wear, construction, agriculture and windblown dust, which means the abatement levers are not the same as for combustion particles. Compare with the dust layer during Saharan intrusions, when natural contributions can be discounted from compliance assessment. Data shown: live, the latest hourly step from the CAMS European regional forecast. Note: modelled forecast at roughly 10 km. Resuspension and local dust sources are the weakest part of any regional PM10 model.

Surface NO2 from the CAMS European regional ensemble. The annual limit value falls to 20 µg/m³ from 2030 under Directive (EU) 2024/2881, against a WHO 2021 guideline of 10 µg/m³. NO2 is the pollutant most directly tied to road transport, so the map reads as a map of traffic and shipping. Compare it with the Sentinel-5P annual column in the greenhouse gases group to see the same combustion signal from two different vantage points, one modelled at the surface and one measured from orbit through the whole troposphere. Data shown: live, the latest hourly step from the CAMS European regional forecast. Note: modelled forecast at roughly 10 km. NO2 gradients across a city are steep and this resolution smooths away the roadside exceedances that drive most compliance failures.

Surface ozone from the CAMS European regional ensemble. Ozone is not emitted. It forms in sunlight from NOx and volatile organic compounds, which makes it the one regulated pollutant that cannot be fixed by acting on a single local source, and the one that gets worse in heatwaves. Southern Europe and downwind rural areas often exceed while city centres do not, because fresh NO from traffic destroys ozone locally. Data shown: live, the latest hourly step from the CAMS European regional forecast. Note: modelled forecast at roughly 10 km. Ozone chemistry is non-linear, so cutting NOx can raise urban ozone in the short term before it falls, which matters when reading this layer as evidence for a policy choice.

Surface SO2 from the CAMS European regional ensemble. SO2 is the clearest success story in European air quality policy, cut by around 90 per cent since 1990 through flue gas desulphurisation and the move away from coal and high-sulphur fuel oil. What remains concentrates around the few large combustion plants and refineries still in operation, plus shipping outside the sulphur emission control areas. It is a useful layer for arguing that regulation demonstrably works. Data shown: live, the latest hourly step from the CAMS European regional forecast. Note: modelled forecast at roughly 10 km. Concentrations are low enough across most of Europe that the map reads as near-empty, which is the point rather than a rendering fault.

Surface ammonia from the CAMS European regional ensemble. Ammonia is not itself subject to an ambient limit value, but it is capped under the National Emission reduction Commitments Directive and it reacts with nitric and sulphuric acid to form secondary inorganic aerosol, a large share of European PM2.5. It is the pollutant where reductions have stalled hardest, because roughly 90 per cent comes from agriculture rather than from combustion. Toggle it with PM2.5 during a spring fertiliser spreading period to see the connection. Data shown: live, the latest hourly step from the CAMS European regional forecast. Note: modelled forecast at roughly 10 km. Ammonia emissions have strong daily and seasonal cycles tied to farm practice and temperature, which regional models represent only approximately.

Surface carbon monoxide from the CAMS European regional ensemble. CO is a marker of incomplete combustion, which makes it useful for separating residential wood and coal burning from cleaner combustion sources. In much of central and eastern Europe the winter CO pattern follows domestic solid fuel heating rather than traffic, and that distinction changes which policy instrument applies. Data shown: live, the latest hourly step from the CAMS European regional forecast. Note: modelled forecast at roughly 10 km. Ambient CO rarely approaches its limit value in Europe, so treat this as a source-attribution layer rather than a health-risk layer.

A single day of TROPOMI tropospheric NO2, as measured rather than modelled. This is the layer that shows what independent observation adds to a reporting system: shipping lanes, individual power stations and city plumes appear without any prior assumption about where emissions should be. The 2020 lockdowns were quantified from exactly this product. Data shown: fixed at 27 July 2026. The underlying GIBS record runs from 6 May 2018 to the present, so the date in the tile URL can be changed to any day in that range, but it will not advance by itself. Note: the date is pinned to 27 July 2026. Cloud leaves gaps, and one day of data is weather, not a trend. For the pattern rather than the day, use the Sentinel-5P annual mean in the greenhouse gases group.

TROPOMI total column SO2 for a single day. Satellite SO2 is how large undeclared point sources get found, because smelters, refineries and coal plants produce plumes that are visible from orbit against an otherwise clean background. It is also the standard tool for tracking volcanic degassing and eruption clouds, which matters for aviation and for discounting natural contributions in compliance assessment. Data shown: fixed at 27 July 2026. The underlying GIBS record runs from 6 May 2018 to the present, so the date in the tile URL can be changed but will not advance by itself. Note: the date is pinned to 27 July 2026. SO2 retrieval has a high detection threshold, so only substantial sources appear and an empty map does not mean zero emissions.

Monthly CO emissions from the MERRA-2 reanalysis, which is an emission flux rather than a concentration. Including one flux layer alongside the concentration layers makes the distinction concrete: concentrations are what people breathe and what the law regulates, fluxes are what inventories report and what mitigation policy actually changes. Data shown: fixed at May 2026, the most recent month available in GIBS when the config was built. MERRA-2 monthly products lag the present by two to three months and this date does not advance by itself. Note: reanalysis emissions are built from inventories and burned-area products, so this is a modelled estimate constrained by observations rather than an independent measurement. Global coverage at coarse resolution.

Dust aerosol optical depth at 550 nm from CAMS, global and updated three-hourly. Saharan dust intrusions push PM10 above the daily limit value across southern Europe several times a year. The Ambient Air Quality Directive allows member states to subtract contributions from natural sources when assessing compliance, and this layer is the kind of evidence used to justify that subtraction. Data shown: live, the latest step from the rolling CAMS global forecast. Note: optical depth is a measure of the whole atmospheric column, so a high value does not automatically mean high concentrations at ground level. Confirming the surface impact needs the PM10 layer alongside it.

Total aerosol optical depth from combined MODIS Terra and Aqua retrievals for a single day. This is the general-purpose haze layer: it responds to wildfire smoke, dust, industrial haze and shipping without distinguishing between them. Data shown: fixed at 27 July 2026. Change the date in the tile URL to move it; it does not advance by itself. Note: the date is pinned to 27 July 2026. MODIS AOD is not retrieved over cloud or over bright surfaces such as snow and desert, which is why gaps appear over exactly the dust sources you might want to see.

Monthly mean aerosol optical depth from the MERRA-2 reanalysis, which fills the gaps that daily satellite retrievals leave. The MERRA-2 record runs from 1980, so this is the layer for aerosol trends over four decades rather than a single episode. Data shown: fixed at May 2026. The MERRA-2 record begins in January 1980, so earlier months can be requested by changing the date in the tile URL. Note: the date is pinned to May 2026. Reanalysis blends model and observations, so it is complete everywhere but less accurate than a direct retrieval where retrievals exist.

The OMPS UV aerosol index tuned for pyrocumulonimbus events, where wildfires generate their own storm clouds and loft smoke into the upper troposphere and stratosphere. Smoke injected that high travels between continents, which turns a national wildfire into someone else's air quality problem and complicates the attribution of an exceedance. Data shown: fixed at 28 July 2026, which is an ordinary day with no major event over Europe. Change the date in the tile URL to a known fire episode to make this layer show something. Note: the date is pinned to 28 July 2026 and Europe will usually be empty. Set the date to a major fire episode to see the signal. The aerosol index is a qualitative indicator of absorbing aerosol, not a concentration.

Near-real-time active fire detection from the Meteosat SEVIRI 3.9 micron channel, covering Europe and Africa. Geostationary detection updates every 15 minutes, which is what makes it useful for the operational side of a smoke episode rather than the retrospective side. Data shown: live, the latest SEVIRI scan. Meteosat updates every 15 minutes. Note: SEVIRI has a coarse footprint compared with polar-orbiting fire products, so it detects large and hot fires and misses small ones. Detection degrades under cloud.

Ground-level NO2 as a three-year running mean for 1996 to 1998, from the SEDAC global surface NO2 dataset derived from satellite columns and chemical transport modelling. This is the before half of a policy evaluation pair. Data shown: fixed. A three-year mean covering 1996 to 1998, a static product with no time dimension. Note: a three-year mean at coarse resolution, so it supports statements about regions and decades, not about streets or single years.

Ground-level NO2 as a three-year running mean for 2010 to 2012, on the same scale as the 1996 to 1998 layer. Across western Europe and North America the decline over those fourteen years is visible without any statistical treatment, while parts of Asia move the other way. That contrast is the clearest single piece of evidence in this explorer that emission standards changed outcomes. Data shown: fixed. A three-year mean covering 2010 to 2012, a static product with no time dimension. Note: same coarse resolution and averaging caveats as the earlier epoch. The two epochs share a method, which is what makes the comparison fair.

A swipe comparison of ground-level NO2 between 1996-98 and 2010-12 on a single map. Drag the divider across western Europe to show the decline, then across east and south Asia to show the increase over the same period. Data shown: fixed. Two static three-year means, 1996 to 1998 on one side and 2010 to 2012 on the other. Note: this is the only swipe layer in the SEF explorer family and it should be checked in GE Preview before the config is shown to an audience. If the swipe control does not appear, use the two standalone epoch layers in this group instead.

Tropospheric NO2 column from OMI on Aura, which has produced a consistent daily record since October 2004. A single instrument spanning more than twenty years is what makes trend attribution defensible, because changes cannot be blamed on a change of sensor. Step the date back to compare the same month across years. Data shown: fixed at 20 July 2026. The OMI record runs from 1 October 2004 to the present, so any day in that span can be requested by changing the date in the tile URL, but it will not advance by itself. Note: the date is pinned to 20 July 2026. OMI has a row anomaly that removes part of each swath from 2007 onwards, and its footprint is much coarser than TROPOMI's, so use OMI for the long record and TROPOMI for detail.

Surface NO2 over Oslo derived from Sentinel-5P TROPOMI, at the resolution the satellite delivers. This is the first half of the argument that satellite data can reach a regulatory question. The values are surface concentrations in µg/m³, the same quantity and units the Ambient Air Quality Directive regulates, rather than the tropospheric column that a raw TROPOMI product reports. Getting there needs a chemistry transport model to supply the vertical distribution, which is why this is a derived product rather than a measurement. Cells are roughly 6 by 8 km over Oslo, so a whole city sits inside a handful of them. Produced by the ESA CitySatAir project (NILU). Data shown: fixed archive. 694 individual overpasses between 4 May 2018 and 19 November 2022. The series has ended and does not extend to the present. Note: each timestep is a single satellite overpass around midday, not a daily or annual mean, so these values cannot be compared with the annual limit value of 20 µg/m³ or with any averaging-period threshold. Use the temporal control to step through 694 overpasses between May 2018 and November 2022. Zoom to Oslo at around 59.9N, 10.8E.

The same Oslo surface NO2 downscaled to roughly 1 km, which is the second half of the argument. Toggle between this layer and the TROPOMI-resolution one to see what downscaling recovers: the coarse product gives a city one value, the downscaled product separates the roads, the port and the residential areas, and the peak concentration rises because it is no longer averaged away. That difference is exactly the gap this explorer's other NO2 layers cannot cross, since CAMS runs at around 10 km and the Sentinel-5P annual mean is a column rather than a surface concentration. Produced by the ESA CitySatAir project (NILU) for the Oslo case study. Data shown: fixed archive. The same 694 overpasses between 4 May 2018 and 19 November 2022. The series has ended and does not extend to the present. Note: downscaling redistributes a satellite-constrained total using proxies and model output, so the fine detail is inferred rather than observed and carries more uncertainty than the coarse field it came from. Some cells are empty where no valid retrieval or model value exists. Single overpasses again, so not comparable with limit values.

Gridded population for Europe from WorldPop. A concentration map alone does not establish harm. Multiplying concentration by the number of people exposed is what converts an air quality field into a health burden and into the cost-benefit terms that abatement policy is argued in. Toggle it under PM2.5 or NO2 to separate a high concentration over farmland from the same concentration over a city. Data shown: fixed, a static file on the SEF bucket. The WorldPop vintage is not recorded in the file name or in the urban explorer that also uses it, so confirm the reference year with the SEF data owner before citing this layer in a document. Note: modelled population distribution built from census data and built-up area, so it carries the uncertainty of both. Europe only.

An aggregated risk index combining modelled air pollution with population, produced under the ESA AlpAirEO project. This is the worked example of the exposure calculation that the population and pollutant layers only imply, delivered as vector units that can be ranked and compared rather than as a raster that has to be read by eye. Ranked units are what a prioritisation discussion needs. Click a unit to read its values. ARI_all, ARI_cardio and ARI_respir are the risk index for all-cause, cardiovascular and respiratory mortality, each paired with the pollutant contributing most to it. HB_dom is the health burden attributable to that pollutant, split between the daytime and the night-time population. The index covers every local administrative unit in EU28+, and Milan and the Lombardy plain carry the highest values in Europe. Data shown: fixed at October 2025, the single snapshot published for this collection in the Project Results Repository. Note: an index is a set of weighting choices, and different weightings produce different rankings, so check the project documentation before using the values to justify a decision. The health burden fields need commuter mobility data, which exists only for Germany and northern Italy, so they read zero elsewhere, and the collection does not state their unit. This is a large file and takes a moment to draw.
